lectures.title: Sending Signals with the `kill` command & the Interruption Signal SIGINT

cues.en: In this lecture, I want to introduce you to the kill command, and let's just have a look.
So you've seen before that we were able to when we were here in our terminal, we were able to enter
Control C to send a signal to a program.
But we want or we can also send signals from other places to a process.
Why would we do that?
Well, maybe not with a Sigint signal.
That was the one we sent before with the keyboard shortcut.
But maybe we want to send different signals.
But before we look at different signals, let's just see how we can send the Sigint from a different
terminal, for example.
So, um, we can also send those signals from other places to a process.
And for this we can use the kill command.
It's important here.
The program, it's just called kill, but it has nothing or well, some of the default are actually
terminating those programs.
But, um, the program is just called kill.
But all it does is to send signals to programs and then those programs or the kernel do the rest.
So it's not actually killing the programs itself.
It's just used to trigger that a signal is being sent to a program.
So we have seen before how we can send the Sigint signal through the terminal with a keyboard shortcut.
So how do we send this one with the kill command?
The way to go is that we use the kill.
Then we say minus s, then the signal we want to send, and then we need the process ID So first, of
course, we need to get the process ID of the process we would like to send the signal to and then we
can send the signal to the process by specifying the signal we want to send and the process ID or actually
sometimes we also can leave this one out and we can just specify the signal like this.
Um, this is another way to use it.
But this one here is more.
Um, I, I do prefer the first way to write it because it's more clear that this is a parameter, but
this is technically also a parameter.
So it would also work.
Let's just see how this one works.
So first we need to restart our download so it's running again.
So now we can see here the download is running.
Now I go to into another terminal here.
In my case it's just in another tab and I can switch between, but it could also be a new terminal window.
I now need to get the process ID of the Get program, so I use the Pgrep command to get my process ID
here.
Now I can say kill, send the signal of type Sigint to this process and we can see here this now has
been accepted and we can see here this download now has come to an end.
It has come to an end just the same way as if I would have been in this terminal using Ctrl and C to
quit or to cancel this download.
But I have sent the signal now not from this terminal but from this kill command here, and I've used
that to send the signal.
Of course, if I would now restart the download again and I would now like to send another signal here,
the process ID would have changed.
So the way to go here would be if I would want to combine, it would be something like this that we
use those expansions here to get the process ID of the Get program and then send the second signal to
it, the Sigint or the interrupt signal.
It's not the only signal we can send with the kill command.
We can actually send all kinds of different signals with the kill command, all available signals we
can send through this command or we can trigger that it's being sent to the process.
We have just used the Sigint because it's the signal that we've used a lot before.
So I wanted to show you how you can use that with the kill command.
But there are quite a few other signal types that I would like to introduce you to, and we'll start
to have a look at that in the next lecture.
